Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Three former guerrilla leaders -- who helped command what one activist called "one of the most brutal rebel movements in modern days" -- were sentenced Wednesday in Freetown, Sierra Leone, for crimes against humanity. Amputee victims of Sierra Leone's civil war take part in football training at a beach in Freetown. The U.N. Special Court for Sierra Leone found the men guilty in February of crimes that included murder, rape, sexual slavery and forced marriages stemming from a civil war that lasted from March 1991 to January 2002. They were arrested in March 2003, said Peter Anderson, spokesman for the U.N. court. The rebels -- former leaders in the Revolutionary United Front guerrilla movement -- were known for hacking off civilians' hands and feet during the war, which stood out for its viciousness even on a a continent that has suffered many horrific conflicts. Presiding Judge Pierre Boutet of Canada read the sentences. Former Revolutionary United Front "interim leader" Issa Hassan Sesay was sentenced to 52 years in prison, former commander Morris Kallon to 40 years, and former chief of security Augustine Gbao to 25 years. Sesay and Kallon had been found guilty on 16 counts, and Gbao was found guilty on 14. The former rebels received credit for the six years each already has served in prison, Anderson told CNN. He said they will be imprisoned in another country, maybe Rwanda, because the prisons in Sierra Leone do not meet the standards of the U.N. court. Kallon was the only one of the three to express sorrow at his sentencing, Anderson said. "He really had made a genuine expression of remorse," which is considered a stronger statement than regret, the court spokesman added. The court noted several mitigating factors at the sentencing, but "in view of the gravity of the crimes, their impact was limited," a statement from the court said. The court noted that the crimes "were committed upon a massive scale across several districts of Sierra Leone" and that "the impact of all these crimes upon the Sierra Leonean society has been enormous." "The Chamber concluded that the inherent gravity of the criminal acts for which Sesay, Kallon and Gbao have been convicted is exceptionally high," the statement said. Corinne Dufka, a senior researcher in Human Rights Watch's Africa division, had called the verdict "very significant." "The RUF were renowned for leading one of the most brutal rebel movements in modern days. Everyone knows about the signature atrocity of limb amputation, but there was also horrific sexual violence, abductions, use of child soldiers and forced marriages," she told CNN by phone from Senegal in West Africa. Eight people have been convicted of war crimes connected with the conflict -- some on the rebels' side and some on the government's. The U.N. Special Court's mandate is to try only "those who bear greatest responsibility for atrocities committed in Sierra Leone." The trial of Sesay, Kallon and Gbao lasted nearly five years. The three had pleaded not guilty on all counts. The Special Court cannot impose the death penalty. The Revolutionary United Front seized most of Sierra Leone from the government and fought international and African peacekeepers. International forces retook the capital, Freetown, in 2000. The trial of the three former leaders was the last of three to be held at the Special Court. Former Liberian President Charles Taylor is on trial separately at an international court in The Hague, Netherlands, for his role in the conflict. The prosecution rested in the Taylor case in January after a year of presenting its arguments. Sierra Leone is known for its diamond wealth, but 70 percent of the population lives below the poverty line. The Special Court is an independent tribunal established jointly by the United Nations and the Sierra Leone government. It is mandated to bring to justice those most responsible for atrocities committed in Sierra Leone after November 30, 1996.

**U.N. court sentences former Sierra Leone rebel leaders for war crimes**

**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone** — Three former leaders of Sierra Leone’s Revolutionary United Front were sentenced Wednesday by a U.N.-backed court for their roles in a brutal civil war marked by mass killings, amputations, rape and the use of child soldiers.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone sentenced **Issa Sesay**, the former interim leader of the rebel movement, to **52 years in prison**. **Morris Kallon**, a senior RUF commander, received **40 years**, while **Augustine Gbao**, another senior figure in the rebel group, was sentenced to **25 years**.

The men had been convicted of crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during Sierra Leone’s 1991-2002 civil war, one of West Africa’s most vicious conflicts. Judges found them responsible for acts including murder, rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, enslavement, looting and the recruitment and use of child soldiers.

Prosecutors said the Revolutionary United Front terrorized civilians as it fought to control diamond-rich areas of the country. The rebel group became notorious for hacking off victims’ limbs, burning villages and forcing children to fight.

The court said the sentences reflected the gravity of the crimes and the suffering inflicted on civilians across Sierra Leone.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone was established jointly by the United Nations and the Sierra Leonean government to try those bearing the greatest responsibility for atrocities committed during the war. Tens of thousands of people were killed, and many more were displaced before the conflict ended in 2002.

The case was among the court’s most significant prosecutions, targeting the senior leadership of the RUF. Human rights groups have described the verdicts and sentences as an important step toward accountability for victims of the conflict.

The three men are expected to serve their sentences outside Sierra Leone under enforcement agreements with other countries.

**RUF Leaders Sentenced in Freetown for Sierra Leone War Atrocities**

**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone —** Three former leaders of Sierra Leone’s Revolutionary United Front were sentenced in Freetown for their roles in a campaign of terror that devastated the country during its civil war, including killings, mutilations, sexual violence, enslavement and the recruitment of child soldiers.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone handed down lengthy prison terms to **Issa Hassan Sesay**, **Morris Kallon** and **Augustine Gbao**, senior figures in the RUF, the rebel movement notorious for brutal attacks on civilians during the 1991–2002 conflict.

Sesay, who became interim leader of the RUF after the arrest of Foday Sankoh, received the heaviest sentence — **52 years in prison**. Kallon, a senior commander, was sentenced to **40 years**, while Gbao, described as a key ideologue and senior official within the movement, received **25 years**.

The court found the men responsible for crimes committed across Sierra Leone as the RUF waged a war marked by systematic violence against civilians. Judges cited atrocities including **murder, rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, enslavement, pillage, terrorizing the civilian population and the use of children as fighters**. The RUF became infamous internationally for amputations and other forms of mutilation used to spread fear and control diamond-rich areas.

The sentences followed convictions for **war crimes and crimes against humanity**, as well as other serious violations of international humanitarian law. Prosecutors argued that the three men helped plan, command or support operations in which civilians were deliberately targeted, villages were burned, women and girls were abducted and abused, and children were forced to serve as combatants.

In delivering sentence, the judges emphasized the scale and cruelty of the crimes and the suffering inflicted on victims throughout Sierra Leone. The court also noted the positions of authority held by the defendants within the RUF and their involvement in sustaining the rebel organization’s military campaign.

The sentencing was a major moment for the Special Court for Sierra Leone, a hybrid tribunal established jointly by the Sierra Leonean government and the United Nations to prosecute those bearing the greatest responsibility for crimes committed during the civil war. The conflict left tens of thousands dead and displaced large parts of the population, while its atrocities became symbols of the human cost of “blood diamonds” and regional instability in West Africa.

For many survivors, the judgment represented a measure of accountability after years of trauma. Victims’ groups have long described the RUF’s campaign as one of extreme brutality, particularly in rural communities where civilians were subjected to forced labor, sexual violence and mutilation.

The RUF’s founder, **Foday Sankoh**, died in custody before he could be tried. Another major figure linked to the conflict, former Liberian president **Charles Taylor**, was tried separately before the Special Court for supporting the RUF and other armed groups.

The sentences for Sesay, Kallon and Gbao marked one of the most significant rulings against former RUF leaders and reinforced the court’s central message: commanders and political leaders can be held criminally responsible for atrocities committed by forces under their authority.

## U.N.-Backed Court Sentences Former Sierra Leone Rebel Commanders for War Crimes

A United Nations-backed tribunal has sentenced three former commanders of Sierra Leone’s Revolutionary United Front to long prison terms for atrocities committed during the country’s brutal civil war, including murder, rape, sexual slavery, mutilation, forced labor and the recruitment of child soldiers.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone handed down sentences against Issa Sesay, Morris Kallon and Augustine Gbao, senior figures in the rebel movement that terrorized civilians during the 1991–2002 conflict. The court sentenced Sesay, the former interim leader of the RUF, to 52 years in prison; Kallon, a senior commander, to 40 years; and Gbao, a high-ranking security official, to 25 years.

Judges found the men responsible for a campaign of violence that included widespread killings, amputations, burning of villages, enslavement of civilians, and the use of children as fighters. The RUF became notorious for hacking off the limbs of civilians, abducting women and girls, forcing prisoners to mine diamonds, and turning boys into combatants.

Prosecutors said the commanders played central roles in organizing and sustaining the rebel war effort, which was funded in part by Sierra Leone’s diamond trade. The conflict, often described as a “blood diamond” war, devastated the West African nation and left tens of thousands dead. More than two million people were displaced.

The civil war began in 1991, when the RUF, led by Foday Sankoh and backed at times by forces from neighboring Liberia, launched an insurgency against Sierra Leone’s government. What began as a rebellion against corruption and poor governance quickly became one of the most violent conflicts of the late 20th century. Rebel forces seized diamond-producing areas and used the profits to buy weapons, while civilians bore the brunt of the violence.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone was established jointly by the United Nations and the Sierra Leonean government to prosecute those bearing the greatest responsibility for crimes committed during the war. It was the first international tribunal to sit in the country where the crimes occurred and was seen as a landmark effort to deliver justice for victims.

The sentencing of the RUF commanders marked one of the court’s most significant judgments. Human rights groups welcomed the decision, saying it recognized the suffering of victims and reinforced the principle that military and political leaders can be held accountable for atrocities committed by forces under their control.

The court also prosecuted leaders from other factions, including members of the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council and the Civil Defence Forces, as well as former Liberian President Charles Taylor, who was later convicted for aiding and abetting crimes in Sierra Leone.

Although Sierra Leone has been at peace since 2002, the legacy of the war remains visible in communities affected by displacement, trauma and physical injury. For survivors, the sentences represented a measure of accountability after years of violence that shattered families and communities across the country.

Prosecutors said commanders oversaw a campaign of killings, mutilations, abductions and systematic sexual violence, including the forced “marriage” of women and girls to fighters.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone, a U.N.-backed tribunal set up in Freetown, found that RUF forces used extreme brutality to punish communities, intimidate opponents and conscript fighters, including children. Victims testified about rebels cutting off hands and arms, carving initials into bodies, burning villages and forcing civilians to work in diamond mines.

The conflict, one of West Africa’s most brutal, left tens of thousands dead and displaced more than 2 million people. The RUF began its insurgency in 1991, claiming to oppose government corruption, but became widely known for attacks on civilians and its role in the illicit diamond trade.

Human rights advocates said the verdicts marked a landmark in international justice, particularly for recognizing forced marriage as a distinct crime against humanity. The court’s cases also helped establish accountability for commanders who did not personally commit abuses but were found responsible for directing or enabling them.

The Special Court was created jointly by Sierra Leone and the United Nations to prosecute those bearing the greatest responsibility for crimes committed during the war. Its most prominent defendant, former Liberian President Charles Taylor, was later convicted for aiding and abetting RUF and allied forces and sentenced to 50 years in prison.

**CNN —** The Special Court for Sierra Leone has delivered its final judgment in Freetown-based trials, convicting three former leaders of the Revolutionary United Front for atrocities committed during Sierra Leone’s brutal civil war.

Former RUF interim leader **Issa Sesay**, senior commander **Morris Kallon**, and commander **Augustine Gbao** were found guilty of war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder, rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, mutilation, conscripting child soldiers and attacks on U.N. peacekeepers.

The RUF became notorious during Sierra Leone’s 1991-2002 conflict for a campaign of terror against civilians, including amputations, mass killings and the use of children in combat. The war left tens of thousands dead and displaced more than 2 million people.

Human Rights Watch welcomed the convictions, calling them an important step toward justice for victims of one of West Africa’s most violent conflicts. The group said the verdicts showed that senior commanders could be held accountable for crimes committed by forces under their control.

The case also carries significance beyond Sierra Leone. It is closely linked to the separate trial of former Liberian President **Charles Taylor**, who was accused of backing the RUF with weapons and support in exchange for so-called “blood diamonds.” Taylor’s trial was moved to The Hague for security reasons, although it remained under the authority of the Special Court for Sierra Leone.

Prosecutors alleged Taylor helped fuel the conflict by aiding the rebels as they committed atrocities across Sierra Leone. Taylor denied the charges.

The RUF convictions marked the end of the Special Court’s main trials in Sierra Leone, leaving Taylor’s case as the court’s most high-profile remaining proceeding and a test of whether a former African head of state could be held responsible for crimes committed in a neighboring country.
